text: In the fourth year of King Darius, on the fourth day of the ninth month, the month of Chislev, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah.
Now the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech with their men to entreat the favor of the LORD,

versions.text: Now the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech, along with their men, to entreat the favor of the LORD,
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has "his men" (וַאֲנָשָׁיו, singular suffix); "their men" is a smoothing but "along with" adds bulk. Tightening also improves oral rhythm. A footnote could note the Hebrew reads "his men."

text: and to ask the priests of the house of the LORD of hosts and the prophets, "Should I go on weeping and abstaining in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?"

versions.text: and to ask the priests of the house of the LORD of hosts and the prophets, "Should I mourn and fast in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?"
versions.explanation: אֶבְכֶּה is "weep," and הִנָּזֵר means "abstain/separate oneself," not specifically "fast." The current rendering flattens two distinct verbs and imports "fast" from later verses.

text: Then the word of the LORD of hosts came to me:
Say to all the people of the land and to the priests: When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and the seventh months these seventy years, was it truly for me, for me, that you fasted?

versions.text: Say to all the people of the land and to the priests: When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months these seventy years, was it really for me that you fasted?
versions.explanation: The Hebrew ends with an emphatic "for me, me" (צַמְתֻּנִי אָנִי). Doubling the pronoun captures the emphasis and reads well aloud.

text: And when you eat and when you drink, is it not you yourselves who eat, you yourselves who drink?

versions.text: And when you eat and when you drink, are you not simply eating and drinking for yourselves?
versions.explanation: The Hebrew repeats the emphatic pronoun "you" twice; the current rendering adds "simply ... for yourselves," which is interpretive. The suggested form preserves the parallel structure and the oral cadence.

text: Should you not obey the words the LORD proclaimed through the earlier prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and at ease, with her towns around her, and the Negev and the foothills were settled?

versions.text: Are these not the very words the LORD proclaimed through the earlier prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and at ease, along with the towns around her, and the Negev and the lowland were settled?
versions.explanation: The verse is elliptical; the point is a rebuke about heeding the earlier prophets' words, not merely identifying them. "Foothills" or a footnote is helpful for שְׁפֵלָה, and "with her towns" is tighter for reading aloud.

text: And the word of the LORD came to Zechariah:
Thus says the LORD of hosts: Render true judgments; show kindness and mercy to one another.
Do not oppress the widow or the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor, and do not plot evil against one another in your hearts.
But they refused to pay attention; they turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears so they would not hear.
They made their hearts hard as flint, refusing to hear the law and the words that the LORD of hosts had sent by his Spirit through the earlier prophets. So great wrath came from the LORD of hosts.
"And just as he called and they would not listen, so they called and I would not listen," says the LORD of hosts.

versions.text: "Just as I called and they would not listen, so when they call I will not listen," says the LORD of hosts.
versions.explanation: Two issues: (1) קָרָא is third person ("he called"), not first person; (2) the imperfect יִקְרְאוּ / אֶשְׁמָע here describes past habitual action, as shown by the following narrative verb in v. 14 ("and I drove them out"). Rendering it as a future threat ("when they call I will not listen") misplaces the events, which already occurred in the exile.

text: "I drove them out with a whirlwind among all the nations they had not known, and the land was left desolate behind them, with none passing to and fro. So a pleasant land was made a desolation."

versions.text: "I scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations they had not known, and the land was left desolate behind them, with no one coming or going. So they made the pleasant land a wasteland."
versions.explanation: מֵעֹבֵר וּמִשָּׁב is an idiom for "none passing to and fro"; also the final clause is best read impersonally ("a pleasant land was made desolate") since "they" is ambiguous between exiles and nations. "Drove them out" better renders the storm-verb than "scattered."

versions.text: "I drove them out with a whirlwind among all the nations they had not known, and the land was left desolate behind them, with no one passing through. So a pleasant land was made a desolation."
versions.explanation: מֵעֹבֵר וּמִשָּׁב is the fixed idiom for movement in both directions ("passing to and fro"); "passing through" conveys only one direction and loses the picture of a road emptied of all traffic. "None passing to and fro" also reads with a tighter rhythm for oral delivery.
